The rule of threes: you can survive roughly 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in harsh weather, 3 days without water and 3 weeks without food.
Boiling water for 1 minute kills the germs that make it unsafe to drink. Above about 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil it for 3 minutes.
Sunlight can disinfect water: fill a clear plastic bottle and leave it in full sun for 6 hours, or 2 days if it is cloudy.
Dark, strong-smelling urine is one of the earliest signs of dehydration.
Drinking seawater makes dehydration worse: your kidneys need more water to get rid of the salt than the seawater provides.
Eating snow costs body heat to melt it. Melt it first whenever you can.
Two drops of regular unscented bleach (about 8% chlorine) per litre, left to stand for 30 minutes, makes clear water safer to drink.
Many portable water filters remove bacteria and parasites but not viruses. Boiling or chemical treatment handles viruses.
A handful of dew can be collected at dawn by dragging a cloth through wet grass and wringing it out.
One millimetre of rain falling on one square metre of roof gives one litre of water.
A solar still usually produces less than a cup of water a day. It is a last resort, not a plan.
A clear plastic bag tied around a leafy branch in the sun collects water that the leaves give off.
Iodine water tablets are not recommended for pregnant women or people with thyroid problems.
Three of anything, whether fires, whistle blasts or flashes of light, is a widely recognised distress signal.
SOS in Morse code is three short, three long, three short: ··· −−− ···
A large X laid out on the ground tells aircraft you need medical help; a large V means you need assistance.
A whistle carries much farther than a shout and uses far less energy.
A signal mirror flash can be seen from many kilometres away on a clear day.
Green leaves on a fire make thick white smoke that stands out against a dark forest.
Text messages often get through when phone calls fail on a crowded network.
Amateur radio operators have provided emergency communications in many disasters when phone and internet networks failed.
A hand-crank radio needs no batteries, and in many countries emergency alerts are broadcast on national stations.
Airplane mode and a dim screen can stretch a phone battery many times further.
Telling someone your route and when you'll be back is one of the most effective safety steps there is.
If you're stranded in a car, staying with it usually makes you much easier to find.
In a snowbound car, keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning.
Carbon monoxide has no smell or colour. Never run a generator, grill or camp stove indoors.
Fire needs three things: heat, fuel and oxygen. Take away any one and it goes out.
Birch bark contains natural oils and often burns even when damp.
Resin-rich pine heartwood, called fatwood, lights easily even in wet weather.
Standing dead wood is usually much drier than wood lying on the ground.
Cotton balls smeared with petroleum jelly are a classic fire starter that burns for minutes.
Steel wool touched to the terminals of a 9-volt battery glows and can start a fire.
A magnifying glass, a lens or even a clear bottle of water can focus sunlight onto tinder.
A ferro rod throws very hot sparks and still works when wet.
Dipping match heads in melted wax makes them waterproof.
Glowing embers, not tall flames, are best for cooking.
"Cotton kills" is an old hiker's saying: wet cotton loses most of its insulation.
Wool keeps much of its warmth even when it's wet.
When you sleep outdoors, you lose most of your heat into the cold ground. Insulate beneath you first.
It's a myth that you lose most of your heat through your head: heat loss depends on how much skin is exposed.
Hypothermia starts when your core temperature falls below 35 °C (95 °F).
When a hypothermic person stops shivering, it's a sign of danger, not recovery.
Severely hypothermic people sometimes take off their clothes. It's called paradoxical undressing.
Heat stroke, with a body temperature over about 40 °C and confusion, is a medical emergency.
Never rub frostbitten skin. Rewarm it in warm, not hot, water.
Don't thaw frostbite if there's any chance it will freeze again: refreezing does more damage.
Fresh snow reflects up to 80% of the sun's ultraviolet rays, which is why snow blindness happens.
The Inuit carved snow goggles with narrow slits to protect their eyes from snow glare.
Cold air sinks, so valley bottoms are often colder at night than the slopes above them.
Inside a well-built snow cave, the temperature can stay near 0 °C even when it's far colder outside.
A space blanket works by reflecting your body's radiated heat back to you.
A lean-to shelter should face away from the wind, with the fire in front of the opening.
Count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by 3: that's roughly the distance in kilometres.
"When thunder roars, go indoors": no place outside is truly safe from lightning.
Just 15 cm (6 in) of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet.
About 30 cm (1 ft) of moving water can float many cars.
In an earthquake: drop, cover and hold on.
If the sea suddenly pulls back far from the shore, a tsunami may be coming. Head for high ground.
Above about 2,500 m, altitude sickness becomes a real risk.
At high altitude water boils below 100 °C, so cooking takes longer.
Direct pressure on a wound stops most bleeding.
A tourniquet goes 5 to 7 cm (2 to 3 in) above the wound, never on a joint, and the time it was applied should be noted.
CPR compressions should be about 100 to 120 per minute: the tempo of "Stayin' Alive".
The recovery position keeps the airway of an unconscious, breathing person clear.
Cool a burn under cool running water for 20 minutes. Never use butter or ice.
After a snakebite, keep still and calm. Don't cut the wound or try to suck out venom.
Remove a tick with fine tweezers, pulling straight up, steadily and slowly.
Treat a sore "hot spot" on your foot before it becomes a blister.
Trench foot got its name in World War I; dry socks are the best prevention.
Honey has been used on wounds since ancient times, and medical-grade honey is still used in wound care today.
Soap destroys many viruses by breaking apart their fatty outer layer.
Washing your hands for 20 seconds with soap and water removes most germs.
Dig latrines at least 60 m (200 ft) away from any water source.
In disasters, diarrhoea and dehydration are major killers. Oral rehydration solution saves lives.
Homemade rehydration drink: 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of clean water.
In hot weather, hard work can make you sweat about a litre an hour.
Mosquitoes kill more people than any other animal, mostly by spreading malaria.
The death cap mushroom causes most fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide, and it can look like edible species.
Symptoms of death cap poisoning can take many hours to appear, by which time the liver is already being damaged.
Cattails are sometimes called the supermarket of the swamp: different parts are edible in different seasons.
Acorns are edible once their bitter tannins are soaked out in water.
Every part of the dandelion, from leaves and flowers to roots, is edible.
Stinging nettles lose their sting when cooked and are very nutritious.
Honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs was reportedly still edible after thousands of years.
White rice stores far longer than brown rice, because the oils in brown rice go rancid.
Stored in sealed bags with oxygen absorbers, dry rice and beans can keep for decades.
A bulging or leaking can may contain botulism. Throw it away without tasting.
Stored food follows one simple rule: first in, first out.
A clay pot inside a larger pot, with wet sand between them, can keep food cool without electricity. It's called a zeer pot.
Pemmican, dried meat pounded with fat, could last for months and fed travellers for centuries.
Ship's biscuit, known as hardtack, could last for years on long voyages.
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds more than a million seed samples as a backup for the world's crops.
The North Star, Polaris, sits within about one degree of true north.
In the southern hemisphere, the Southern Cross points toward the south.
Moss grows on every side of trees. It's not a reliable compass.
The shadow-stick trick: mark the tip of a stick's shadow, wait 15 minutes, mark it again. The first mark is west, the second east.
The sun rises exactly in the east and sets exactly in the west only around the equinoxes.
Studies show that people walking without landmarks tend to walk in circles.
With an analogue watch in the northern hemisphere, point the hour hand at the sun: south is halfway between it and 12.
Following water downhill often leads to paths, farms and towns.
Paracord, or 550 cord, holds about 550 pounds, and its inner strands can be pulled out for fishing line or thread.
The bowline knot makes a loop that won't slip, yet it's easy to untie after a heavy load.
Duct tape was developed during World War II to seal ammunition cases.
The Swiss Army knife was first made for Swiss soldiers in 1891.
A small tea-light candle burns for about four hours.
Survival instructors teach STOP when you're lost: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan.
Panic burns energy and clouds judgement. A few slow breaths are a survival tool.
Survivors of extreme situations often say the will to live mattered as much as their gear.
Potassium iodide tablets protect only the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine, not from other radiation.
Fallout radiation drops roughly tenfold for every sevenfold increase in time: the 7-10 rule.
After a nuclear emergency the advice is simple: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.
The middle of a basement or of a large building gives much more protection from fallout than rooms near outside walls.
Wolves, lynx and rare Przewalski's horses now roam the Chernobyl exclusion zone.
The word quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta giorni: forty days.
Keeping a paper map and a compass matters: phones and GPS need power and signal.
